26  Polynomial and Spline Interpolation

Interpolation is the process of constructing a continuous function that passes exactly through a discrete collection of given data points. Given \(n+1\) distinct abscissas (or nodes) \(x_0, x_1, ..., x_n \in \fR\) and corresponding values \(y_0, y_1, ..., y_n \in \fR\), polynomial interpolation seeks a polynomial \(P_n\) of degree at most \(n\) such that \[ \begin{align} P_n(x_i) = y_i, \qquad i = 0, 1, ..., n. \end{align} \] Polynomials are useful local and global approximants because finite polynomial representations can be evaluated, differentiated, and integrated by finite algorithms.

26.1 Existence, Uniqueness, and the Vandermonde Matrix

NoteTheorem: Existence and Uniqueness of the Interpolating Polynomial

Let \(x_0, x_1, ..., x_n\) be \(n+1\) pairwise distinct real numbers, and let \(y_0, y_1, ..., y_n\) be arbitrary real numbers. There exists a unique polynomial \(P_n \in \mathcal{P}_n\) of degree at most \(n\) such that \(P_n(x_i) = y_i\) for all \(i = 0, 1, ..., n\).

TipProof

We establish existence and uniqueness using the fundamental properties of polynomials.

  1. Uniqueness: Suppose there exist two polynomials \(P_n, Q_n \in \mathcal{P}_n\) that satisfy the interpolation conditions, so \(P_n(x_i) = Q_n(x_i) = y_i\) for \(i = 0, ..., n\). Define the difference polynomial \(R(x) = P_n(x) - Q_n(x)\). Because \(\mathcal{P}_n\) is a vector space, \(R\) has degree at most \(n\). Furthermore, \[ \begin{align} R(x_i) = P_n(x_i) - Q_n(x_i) = y_i - y_i = 0, \qquad i = 0, ..., n. \end{align} \] Thus \(R(x)\) has at least \(n+1\) distinct real roots. By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, a non-zero polynomial of degree at most \(n\) can have at most \(n\) roots. Therefore, \(R(x)\) must be the zero polynomial, which implies \(P_n(x) \equiv Q_n(x)\).

  2. Existence via Linear Algebra: Express \(P_n(x)\) in the standard monomial basis: \[ \begin{align} P_n(x) = c_0 + c_1 x + c_2 x^2 + ... + c_n x^n = \sum_{j=0}^n c_j x^j. \end{align} \] The interpolation conditions \(P_n(x_i) = y_i\) form a square \((n+1) \times (n+1)\) linear system \(\bV \bc = \by\): \[ \begin{align} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_0 & x_0^2 & \cdots & x_0^n \\ 1 & x_1 & x_1^2 & \cdots & x_1^n \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n & x_n^2 & \cdots & x_n^n \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} c_0 \\ c_1 \\ \vdots \\ c_n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} y_0 \\ y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{pmatrix}. \end{align} \] The matrix \(\bV\) is the Vandermonde matrix. Its determinant evaluates to \[ \begin{align} \det(\bV) = \prod_{0 \leq i < j \leq n} (x_j - x_i). \end{align} \] Because the nodes \(x_i\) are pairwise distinct, \(x_j - x_i \neq 0\) for all \(j > i\), so \(\det(\bV) \neq 0\). Consequently, \(\bV\) is invertible, and a unique coefficient vector \(\bc = \bV^{-1} \by\) exists for any data vector \(\by\).

TipRemark

Although the Vandermonde matrix provides a constructive proof of existence, solving \(\bV\bc=\by\) in the monomial basis is often a poor numerical representation. Its condition number depends on the nodes and their scaling and can grow rapidly with degree. A large coefficient error does not imply that the interpolation problem itself is ill-posed: it may instead reflect an ill-conditioned choice of basis. The Lagrange and barycentric forms avoid solving for monomial coefficients.

26.2 The Lagrange Form

The Lagrange formulation circumvents the ill-conditioned Vandermonde linear system by constructing a basis of polynomials tailored to the specific nodes \(x_i\).

NoteDefinition: Lagrange Basis Polynomials

Given \(n+1\) distinct nodes \(x_0, x_1, ..., x_n\), the \(i\)-th Lagrange basis polynomial \(L_i \in \mathcal{P}_n\) is defined by \[ \begin{align} L_i(x) = \prod_{\substack{j=0 \\ j \neq i}}^n \frac{x - x_j}{x_i - x_j} = \frac{(x - x_0)\cdots(x - x_{i-1})(x - x_{i+1})\cdots(x - x_n)}{(x_i - x_0)\cdots(x_i - x_{i-1})(x_i - x_{i+1})\cdots(x_i - x_n)}. \end{align} \] The Lagrange basis polynomials satisfy the cardinal Kronecker delta property: \[ \begin{align} L_i(x_j) = \delta_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0, & \text{if } i \neq j. \end{cases} \end{align} \] The interpolating polynomial in Lagrange form is \[ \begin{align} P_n(x) = \sum_{i=0}^n y_i L_i(x). \end{align} \]

NoteExample

To interpolate the three data points \((-1, 1)\), \((0, 0)\), and \((1, 1)\), we construct the degree-2 Lagrange basis polynomials on \(x_0 = -1, x_1 = 0, x_2 = 1\): \[ \begin{align} L_0(x) &= \frac{(x - 0)(x - 1)}{(-1 - 0)(-1 - 1)} = \frac{x(x - 1)}{2} = \frac{x^2 - x}{2}, \\ L_1(x) &= \frac{(x - (-1))(x - 1)}{(0 - (-1))(0 - 1)} = \frac{(x + 1)(x - 1)}{-1} = 1 - x^2, \\ L_2(x) &= \frac{(x - (-1))(x - 0)}{(1 - (-1))(1 - 0)} = \frac{x(x + 1)}{2} = \frac{x^2 + x}{2}. \end{align} \] Multiplying by the data values \(y_0 = 1, y_1 = 0, y_2 = 1\) gives \[ \begin{align} P_2(x) = 1 \cdot \left(\frac{x^2 - x}{2}\right) + 0 \cdot (1 - x^2) + 1 \cdot \left(\frac{x^2 + x}{2}\right) = \frac{x^2 - x + x^2 + x}{2} = x^2. \end{align} \]

TipRemark

The standard Lagrange form has two practical shortcomings. First, evaluating \(P_n(x)\) at a single point \(x\) requires \(O(n^2)\) floating-point operations. Second, adding a new node \((x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\) alters every single basis polynomial \(L_i(x)\), requiring a complete recomputation from scratch.

26.3 The Barycentric Interpolation Formula

Barycentric interpolation reorganizes the Lagrange formula into a stable, computationally optimal form requiring only \(O(n)\) operations per evaluation.

NoteTheorem: Barycentric Interpolation Formulas

Let \(\ell(x) = \prod_{j=0}^n (x - x_j)\) denote the nodal polynomial. For each node \(x_i\), define the barycentric weights \[ \begin{align} w_i = \frac{1}{\prod_{j \neq i} (x_i - x_j)} = \frac{1}{\ell'(x_i)}, \qquad i = 0, 1, ..., n. \end{align} \] Then the interpolating polynomial satisfies:

  1. First Barycentric Form: \[ \begin{align} P_n(x) = \ell(x) \sum_{i=0}^n \frac{w_i}{x - x_i} y_i. \end{align} \]

  2. Second (True) Barycentric Form: \[ \begin{align} P_n(x) = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^n \frac{w_i}{x - x_i} y_i}{\sum_{i=0}^n \frac{w_i}{x - x_i}}. \end{align} \]

If \(x = x_j\) for some node index \(j\), the formula evaluates to \(P_n(x_j) = y_j\).

TipProof

We express the Lagrange basis polynomials in terms of \(\ell(x)\) and \(w_i\). By definition, \[ \begin{align} L_i(x) = \prod_{j \neq i} \frac{x - x_j}{x_i - x_j} = \left( \prod_{j \neq i} (x - x_j) \right) \left( \frac{1}{\prod_{j \neq i} (x_i - x_j)} \right) = \frac{\ell(x)}{x - x_i} w_i. \end{align} \] Substituting this relation into \(P_n(x) = \sum_{i=0}^n y_i L_i(x)\) yields the First Barycentric Formula: \[ \begin{align} P_n(x) = \sum_{i=0}^n y_i \left( \frac{\ell(x)}{x - x_i} w_i \right) = \ell(x) \sum_{i=0}^n \frac{w_i}{x - x_i} y_i. \end{align} \] To derive the Second Barycentric Formula, consider interpolating the constant function \(f(x) \equiv 1\), where \(y_i = 1\) for all \(i\). Because the unique degree-\(n\) interpolant of a constant is the constant itself, the First Barycentric Formula gives \[ \begin{align} 1 = \ell(x) \sum_{i=0}^n \frac{w_i}{x - x_i}. \end{align} \] Dividing the expression for \(P_n(x)\) by this identity cancels the nodal polynomial \(\ell(x)\), yielding \[ \begin{align} P_n(x) = \frac{P_n(x)}{1} = \frac{\ell(x) \sum_{i=0}^n \frac{w_i}{x - x_i} y_i}{\ell(x) \sum_{i=0}^n \frac{w_i}{x - x_i}} = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^n \frac{w_i}{x - x_i} y_i}{\sum_{i=0}^n \frac{w_i}{x - x_i}}. \end{align} \]

TipRemark

The Second Barycentric Formula enjoys extraordinary numerical stability. As proven by Higham (2004), barycentric interpolation is backward stable: the computed value \(\hat{P}_n(x)\) is the exact value of a polynomial interpolating slightly perturbed data \(y_i(1 + \varepsilon_i)\). Furthermore, common multiplicative factors in the weights \(w_i\) cancel out in the numerator and denominator, allowing simple analytical expressions for standard node families (such as Chebyshev nodes).

26.4 The Interpolation Error Formula

NoteTheorem: Cauchy Remainder Error Theorem

Let \(f \in C^{n+1}[a, b]\), and let \(P_n \in \mathcal{P}_n\) interpolate \(f\) at \(n+1\) distinct nodes \(x_0, x_1, ..., x_n \in [a, b]\). For each point \(x \in [a, b]\), there exists a point \(\xi_x \in (a, b)\) such that \[ \begin{align} f(x) - P_n(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_x)}{(n+1)!} \prod_{j=0}^n (x - x_j) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_x)}{(n+1)!} \omega_{n+1}(x), \end{align} \] where \(\omega_{n+1}(x) = \prod_{j=0}^n (x - x_j)\) is the nodal error polynomial.

TipProof

If \(x = x_i\) for some node \(x_i\), both sides vanish and the formula holds trivially for any \(\xi_x\). Now fix \(x \in [a, b]\) with \(x \neq x_i\) for all \(i\). Define the constant \[ \begin{align} \lambda = \frac{f(x) - P_n(x)}{\omega_{n+1}(x)}, \end{align} \] and consider the auxiliary function \(g : [a, b] \to \fR\) defined by \[ \begin{align} g(t) = f(t) - P_n(t) - \lambda \omega_{n+1}(t). \end{align} \] Because \(f \in C^{n+1}[a, b]\) and polynomials are infinitely differentiable, \(g \in C^{n+1}[a, b]\). We evaluate \(g\) at the \(n+2\) distinct points \(x_0, x_1, ..., x_n\) and \(x\): \[ \begin{align} g(x_i) &= f(x_i) - P_n(x_i) - \lambda \omega_{n+1}(x_i) = y_i - y_i - 0 = 0, \qquad i = 0, ..., n, \\ g(x) &= f(x) - P_n(x) - \left( \frac{f(x) - P_n(x)}{\omega_{n+1}(x)} \right) \omega_{n+1}(x) = 0. \end{align} \] Thus \(g(t)\) vanishes at \(n+2\) distinct points in \([a, b]\).

By Rolle’s Theorem, between any two adjacent zeros of \(g(t)\), its derivative \(g'(t)\) has at least one zero. Therefore, \(g'(t)\) has at least \(n+1\) distinct zeros in \((a, b)\). Applying Rolle’s Theorem successively:

  • \(g''(t)\) has at least \(n\) distinct zeros in \((a, b)\),

  • \(g'''(t)\) has at least \(n-1\) distinct zeros in \((a, b)\),

  • Continuing inductively, \(g^{(n+1)}(t)\) has at least one zero in \((a, b)\), which we denote by \(\xi_x\).

We now differentiate \(g(t)\) exactly \(n+1\) times with respect to \(t\): \[ \begin{align} g^{(n+1)}(t) = f^{(n+1)}(t) - P_n^{(n+1)}(t) - \lambda \frac{d^{n+1}}{dt^{n+1}} [\omega_{n+1}(t)]. \end{align} \] Since \(P_n\) has degree at most \(n\), its \((n+1)\)-th derivative is identically zero: \(P_n^{(n+1)}(t) \equiv 0\). The nodal polynomial \(\omega_{n+1}(t) = t^{n+1} + ...\) is a monic polynomial of degree \(n+1\), so its \((n+1)\)-th derivative is \((n+1)!\). Evaluating at \(t = \xi_x\) gives \[ \begin{align} 0 = g^{(n+1)}(\xi_x) = f^{(n+1)}(\xi_x) - 0 - \lambda (n+1)!. \end{align} \] Solving for \(\lambda\) produces \[ \begin{align} \lambda = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_x)}{(n+1)!}. \end{align} \] Equating this to our definition of \(\lambda = (f(x) - P_n(x)) / \omega_{n+1}(x)\) completes the proof.

26.5 Runge’s Phenomenon and Chebyshev Nodes

The error bound contains two decoupled components: \[ \begin{align} \|f - P_n\|_\infty \leq \frac{\|f^{(n+1)}\|_\infty}{(n+1)!} \|\omega_{n+1}\|_\infty. \end{align} \] The derivative term \(\|f^{(n+1)}\|_\infty\) depends entirely on the analytical smoothness of \(f\), while \(\|\omega_{n+1}\|_\infty = \max_{x \in [a, b]} |\prod_{j=0}^n (x - x_j)|\) depends exclusively on the geometric placement of the interpolation nodes.

TipRemark

(Runge phenomenon) Analyticity alone does not make equally spaced interpolation converge. For Runge’s function \(f(x)=1/(1+25x^2)\), the interpolants on equally spaced nodes develop increasing endpoint oscillations and satisfy \[ \begin{align} \lim_{n \to \infty} \|f - P_n\|_\infty = \infty, \end{align} \] even though \(f\) is analytic on the real interval. The growing Lebesgue constant amplifies the approximation error, while the nearby complex poles at \(\pm i/5\) limit the rate of polynomial approximation. The derivative remainder bound above warns that convergence is not automatic, but a divergent upper bound by itself would not prove divergence.

NoteTheorem: Chebyshev Node Optimality

The Chebyshev nodes on \([-1, 1]\) are defined by \[ \begin{align} x_k = \cos\left( \frac{2k+1}{2n+2} \pi \right), \qquad k = 0, 1, ..., n. \end{align} \] They are the roots of the degree-\((n+1)\) Chebyshev polynomial \(T_{n+1}(x) = \cos((n+1)\arccos x)\). The associated nodal polynomial is \[ \begin{align} \omega_{n+1}(x) = \prod_{k=0}^n (x - x_k) = 2^{-n} T_{n+1}(x). \end{align} \] Among all possible choices of \(n+1\) nodes on \([-1, 1]\), Chebyshev nodes minimize the maximum absolute value of the nodal polynomial: \[ \begin{align} \|\omega_{n+1}\|_\infty = \max_{x \in [-1, 1]} |\omega_{n+1}(x)| = 2^{-n}. \end{align} \] If \(f\) extends analytically to a complex neighborhood of \([-1,1]\), polynomial interpolation at Chebyshev nodes converges geometrically, with the nearest complex singularity determining the rate.

TipRemark

The Lebesgue constant \(\Lambda_n = \max_{x \in [a, b]} \sum_{i=0}^n |L_i(x)|\) bounds the stability of polynomial interpolation: \(\|f - P_n\|_\infty \leq (1 + \Lambda_n) \min_{Q \in \mathcal{P}_n} \|f - Q\|_\infty\).

  • For equally spaced nodes, \(\Lambda_n \sim O\left(\frac{2^n}{n \log n}\right)\) grows exponentially.

  • For Chebyshev nodes, \(\Lambda_n \sim \frac{2}{\pi} \log(n+1) + O(1)\) grows only logarithmically, remaining near-optimal.

26.6 Piecewise Polynomials: Cubic Splines

When interpolating large sets of experimental data without prior knowledge of analytical smoothness, high-degree global polynomials are abandoned in favor of piecewise low-degree polynomials. A spline is a piecewise polynomial that maintains global derivative continuity across all internal nodes.

NoteDefinition: Cubic Spline Interpolant

Given \(n+1\) distinct points \(a = x_0 < x_1 < ... < x_n = b\) and values \(y_0, y_1, ..., y_n\), a cubic spline \(S(x)\) is a function such that:

  1. On each subinterval \([x_i, x_{i+1}]\), \(S(x) = S_i(x)\) is a cubic polynomial: \[ \begin{align} S_i(x) = a_i + b_i(x - x_i) + c_i(x - x_i)^2 + d_i(x - x_i)^3, \qquad i = 0, ..., n-1. \end{align} \]

  2. Interpolation conditions: \(S(x_i) = y_i\) for all \(i = 0, ..., n\).

  3. \(C^2\) continuity: \(S(x)\), \(S'(x)\), and \(S''(x)\) are continuous on the entire interval \([a, b]\).

NoteTheorem: The Tridiagonal Spline System

Let \(h_i = x_{i+1} - x_i\) and let \(M_i = S''(x_i)\) denote the second derivative of the spline at node \(x_i\). The condition that \(S'(x)\) is continuous at each interior node \(x_i\) (\(i = 1, ..., n-1\)) leads to the linear system \[ \begin{align} h_{i-1} M_{i-1} + 2(h_{i-1} + h_i) M_i + h_i M_{i+1} = 6 \left( \frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{h_i} - \frac{y_i - y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}} \right). \end{align} \] To close the system of \(n-1\) equations in \(n+1\) unknowns, two boundary conditions are imposed:

  1. Natural (Free) Spline: \(M_0 = M_n = 0\).

  2. Clamped (Complete) Spline: \(S'(x_0) = f'(a)\) and \(S'(x_n) = f'(b)\).

  3. Periodic Spline: \(S'(x_0) = S'(x_n)\) and \(M_0 = M_n\).

For natural and clamped boundary conditions, the resulting linear system is strictly diagonally dominant and symmetric positive definite. It can be solved in \(O(n)\) time using the Thomas algorithm.

TipProof

Since \(S_i(x)\) is a cubic polynomial on \([x_i, x_{i+1}]\), its second derivative \(S_i''(x)\) is a linear function interpolating \(M_i = S''(x_i)\) and \(M_{i+1} = S''(x_{i+1})\): \[ \begin{align} S_i''(x) = M_i \frac{x_{i+1} - x}{h_i} + M_{i+1} \frac{x - x_i}{h_i}. \end{align} \] Integrating twice with respect to \(x\) gives \[ \begin{align} S_i(x) = \frac{M_i (x_{i+1} - x)^3}{6 h_i} + \frac{M_{i+1} (x - x_i)^3}{6 h_i} + C_i (x_{i+1} - x) + D_i (x - x_i). \end{align} \] Applying the interpolation conditions \(S_i(x_i) = y_i\) and \(S_i(x_{i+1}) = y_{i+1}\) determines the constants \(C_i\) and \(D_i\): \[ \begin{align} C_i = \frac{y_i}{h_i} - \frac{M_i h_i}{6}, \qquad D_i = \frac{y_{i+1}}{h_i} - \frac{M_{i+1} h_i}{6}. \end{align} \] Differentiating \(S_i(x)\) to obtain \(S_i'(x)\) and evaluating at the endpoints of \([x_i, x_{i+1}]\) yields \[ \begin{align} S_i'(x_i) &= -\frac{M_i h_i}{3} - \frac{M_{i+1} h_i}{6} + \frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{h_i}, \\ S_{i-1}'(x_i) &= \frac{M_{i-1} h_{i-1}}{6} + \frac{M_i h_{i-1}}{3} + \frac{y_i - y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}. \end{align} \] Equating \(S_{i-1}'(x_i) = S_i'(x_i)\) for continuity of the first derivative and gathering terms produces the stated tridiagonal equation. Strict diagonal dominance follows from \(2(h_{i-1} + h_i) > h_{i-1} + h_i\), which guarantees non-singularity and unconditional stability of Gaussian elimination without pivoting.

NoteTheorem: Minimum Curvature (Energy Minimization) Property

Let \(S(x)\) be the natural cubic spline interpolating \(f(x)\) at \(x_0, x_1, ..., x_n\). Let \(g \in C^2[a, b]\) be any other function satisfying \(g(x_i) = y_i\) for all \(i = 0, ..., n\). Then \[ \begin{align} \int_a^b [S''(x)]^2\,dx \leq \int_a^b [g''(x)]^2\,dx. \end{align} \] Natural cubic splines are the smoothest possible interpolants in the sense of minimizing total bending energy.

TipProof

Let \(h(x) = g(x) - S(x)\). Since both \(g\) and \(S\) interpolate \(f\) at the knots \(x_0, x_1, ..., x_n\), we have \[ \begin{align} h(x_i) = g(x_i) - S(x_i) = y_i - y_i = 0, \qquad i = 0, 1, ..., n. \end{align} \] Expanding the squared second derivative of \(g = S + h\): \[ \begin{align} \int_a^b [g''(x)]^2\,dx &= \int_a^b [S''(x) + h''(x)]^2\,dx \\ &= \int_a^b [S''(x)]^2\,dx + 2\int_a^b S''(x)h''(x)\,dx + \int_a^b [h''(x)]^2\,dx. \end{align} \] We evaluate the cross term by integrating by parts on each subinterval \([x_i, x_{i+1}]\): \[ \begin{align} \int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}} S''(x)h''(x)\,dx &= \left[ S''(x) h'(x) \right]_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}} - \int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}} S'''(x) h'(x)\,dx. \end{align} \] Because \(S(x)\) is a cubic polynomial on \([x_i, x_{i+1}]\), its third derivative \(S_i'''(x)\) is constant on \((x_i, x_{i+1})\). Let \(S_i'''(x) = c_i\). Then \[ \begin{align} \int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}} S'''(x) h'(x)\,dx &= c_i \int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}} h'(x)\,dx = c_i [h(x_{i+1}) - h(x_i)] = 0, \end{align} \] since \(h(x_{i+1}) = h(x_i) = 0\). Summing the boundary terms over all subintervals: \[ \begin{align} \int_a^b S''(x)h''(x)\,dx &= \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \left( S''(x_{i+1}^-) h'(x_{i+1}) - S''(x_i^+) h'(x_i) \right) \\ &= S''(b) h'(b) - S''(a) h'(a) + \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \left( S''(x_i^-) - S''(x_i^+) \right) h'(x_i). \end{align} \] Because \(S \in C^2[a, b]\), the second derivative is continuous across interior knots: \(S''(x_i^-) - S''(x_i^+) = 0\). For a natural cubic spline, \(S''(a) = S''(b) = 0\), so the boundary terms vanish as well. Therefore \[ \begin{align} \int_a^b S''(x)h''(x)\,dx = 0. \end{align} \] Substituting this back yields \[ \begin{align} \int_a^b [g''(x)]^2\,dx &= \int_a^b [S''(x)]^2\,dx + \int_a^b [h''(x)]^2\,dx \geq \int_a^b [S''(x)]^2\,dx, \end{align} \] with equality if and only if \(h''(x) \equiv 0\), meaning \(h\) is linear and hence identically zero because \(h(x_0) = h(x_n) = 0\).

26.7 Exercises

WarningExercise

  1. Compute. Let \(x_0 = 0, x_1 = 1, x_2 = 3\) and \(y_0 = 1, y_1 = 3, y_2 = 2\). Construct the interpolating polynomial \(P_2(x)\) using:

    1. The Vandermonde matrix system.

    2. The Lagrange basis form.

    3. The Barycentric formula.

      Verify that all three approaches yield identical polynomials.

  2. Derive. Compute the barycentric weights \(w_0, ..., w_n\) explicitly for \(n+1\) Chebyshev nodes on \([-1, 1]\). Show that \(w_k = (-1)^k \sin\left(\frac{2k+1}{2n+2}\pi\right)\) (or \((-1)^k \delta_k\) with \(\delta_k = 1/2\) at boundary nodes for Chebyshev-Lobatto points).

  3. Check. Use the result above to bound the maximum error when \(f(x) = \sin(x)\) is interpolated by a polynomial of degree 4 on \([0, \pi/2]\) using equally spaced nodes.

  4. Compute. Set up the \(2 \times 2\) tridiagonal linear system for the natural cubic spline interpolating \((0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0), (3, 1)\). Solve for \(M_1\) and \(M_2\), and write down the explicit cubic polynomial for each subinterval.

  5. Explore. For the spline in the previous exercise, compute its bending energy \(\int_0^3(S'')^2\,dx\) and compare it with the energy of one other twice-differentiable interpolant.
